Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to table a copy in English and in French of order in council P.C. 1955-308 of March 1, 1955, appointing a royal commission on the coasting trade of Canada. The terms of reference will be found in the order in council, but in broad language they direct inquiry into all questions within the jurisdiction of parliament arising out of the water transport of goods and passengers from one place in Canada to another place in Canada, including the great lakes.
Attention is specifically directed to such matters as the relationship between Canada's coasting trade and the shipping and ship building industries, the relation to domestic and international trade generally, the probable effects of the St. Lawrence seaway on the coasting trade, the effects of participation in the coasting trade of vessels or other marine craft not built or registered in Canada, and the desirability, if any, of establishing different policies with respect to the coasting trade for particular parts of Canada.

1.	What are the regulations now in effect respecting the acceptance by Canadians of decorations from foreign governments?
2.	Have any awards been made to Canadians by foreign governments in the last year, in which there has been no compliance with Canadian regulations? If so, by which foreign governments?

This question, as indicated on the order paper, is to be answered orally. The first part of the question is as follows:
What are the regulations now in effect respecting the acceptance by Canadians of decorations from foreign governments?
The policy of the Canadian government, which has been for some years made known to foreign governments through their diplomatic representatives in Ottawa, is opposed to their awarding decorations to Canadians except for (a) gallantry in the rescue or attempt to rescue human lives in danger or (b) services rendered in connection with military operations, the latest instances of this category of service being those with respect to the United Nations operations in Korea. Any foreign government wishing to award a decoration to a Canadian is expected, under this policy, to seek beforehand the agreement of the Canadian government through the Department of External Affairs.
With reference to the second part of the question, the answer is that the Canadian government has no official information regarding foreign decorations, if any, awarded to Canadians in the last year by foreign governments contrary to the policy outlined in the answer I have just given. The Canadian government's attention has been called to reports in the press regarding two cases, and inquiries have been made about them. Pending the results of these inquiries, it is felt that it would not be appropriate for the Canadian government to give any details.

Arising out of the Prime Minister's oral answer to this question I should like to ask, has there been any communication by the government of Canada with any foreign government with reference to the award of any decoration, as reported in the press, that was awarded without the consent of the Canadian government?

The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Harris for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mrs. Fairclough.

Mr. Speaker, last evening when the house closed at ten o'clock we were discussing a subject that every member in the house considers of extreme importance, namely the unemployment situation now existing in this country.
During my remarks I was asked on several occasions by those who had preceded me in the debate what the program of the social credit party is. I promised at that time I would give a program that we would consider sufficient to meet the existing emergency. But the amazing thing was that those who were asking me to produce a program, although they had spoken before me for their allotted time, failed completely to give a program of their own.
The only program that has been given in the house up to this time is the one presented

Unemployment
by the Liberal party, and that program was certainly not satisfactory. They said in effect that they were going to continue the same type of program they were then pursuing, and if the matter got worse-because they did not consider it overly bad at the moment -they then might take other measures.
Of course we all know that the program the Liberal party has been pursuing is the same program they followed before, during the first great depression in the thirties; and the only way we got out of that depression was through preparations for war. Today they are pursuing the same policy and the same program they have pursued since the last war, a policy which has led us to the point where we now have over 600,000 unemployed.
The Progressive Conservatives would follow the same type of policy as the Liberals, only they say they would do it better than the Liberals. But when they were in power they failed under their program to get us out of the depression. So we have not much hope there. They seem to be wandering in a whirlpool of confusion, knowing neither where they are going nor what they would do when they get there.
Then we have the socialists, representatives of whom have spoken in this debate. They, too, have failed to point out any program they would follow, other than saying that they would give us a socialist platform. And the socialist platform they would follow would be the socialist platform that was followed in New Zealand, Australia and Great Britain, and in Saskatchewan. That program proved to be a failure in every instance and, in the countries I have mentioned, it was kicked out and supplanted by that of another party.
I am informed by the whip of this party that I have not very much time left at my disposal. I do not wish to be accused of making a speech and not giving our program.
Five minutes.
We must have written that.

I hear some of my socialist friends saying, "That is what we would do." Well, they are the biggest copycats we ever saw. Whenever there is anything good given out they say, "Oh, that's what we would do." But, in actual fact, what they would do is exactly the same as any other socialist-minded party would do: They would socialize everything, even the means of life.
And the farms, too.

Now, I shall not have time to deal with all the points I have mentioned, but I can assure the house that members of the social credit party will discuss them in detail as this debate goes on.
In the time left to me I would refer to point number 4, which refers to a vigorous construction program. I have indicated on other occasions, as other hon. members have, that there should be a vigorous construction program in the home building industry, and for a moment I would refer to that. I think there is no other program that could be instituted which would give more employment to a greater number of people at a satisfactory wage than the construction of homes. I believe this is generally agreed by all those who have anything to do with this kind of work.
We must understand that one of the things most needed in this country at the present time is better homes for those who wish to have them but are unable to finance them. The present plan of the government for national housing is one which will cover only a very small proportion of the people in this country. Certainly the down payment in itself excludes at least 75 per cent of the people in Canada who really need homes.
On other occasions we have suggested a full plan for housing. Let me review in just a few words what we have said. I have pointed

out that the federal government should set up a fund which it could get from the Bank of Canada at an interest rate of not more than 2 per cent.
That is more of the C.C.F. program.
You stole that from us, too.
That is why you have nothing left.
Perhaps the socialists could start those big sawmills operating and give the home builders a decent price on lumber.
They are operating.

And don't make any mistake about it, they are making a profit from it, too.
But let me say that if the federal government would set up this fund and lend the money to the municipalities at not more than 2 per cent, such loans being guaranteed by the provinces, the municipalities could then go ahead and construct the kind of homes that would be suitable in a particular locality. I am sure that under those circumstances a great number of people would begin building homes immediately, and there would be many jobs available for people who are not now working. If that were done it would create jobs for those who are in need of them. And, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say this, that anyone wishing to have more detailed information in regard to housing need only read from Hansard what I have said on other occasions.
We believe sincerely that the program we have indicated to the house at this time will take care of the immediate problem of unemployment now facing us. If the hon. members, particularly those in the Conservative ranks, and more particularly those in the socialist ranks-and I emphasize that-would rise in their places and lay down a policy that could be followed, then I am sure that this country would be appreciative of it. So far we are still waiting for them. I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that when we are finished this debate the country will not be lacking information on how to solve this economic problem of unemployment.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposiiion):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I read with interest in the press today some of the reports of the debate that took place yesterday, and I was interested to find that this was interpreted as a resolution calling for the overthrow of the federal government because of rising unemployment. I assure you that even with the kindness that has been extended to me
Unemployment
on this and on other occasions, I would regard that as a very happy outcome. Nevertheless, I have not thought, nor has any other hon. member, that suddenly such a wave of changing opinion is going to sweep across the ranks of the large majority opposite that this outcome, desirable though it may be, is likely to be achieved at this time.
It is of course quite proper to describe a motion of this kind as a want of confidence motion; but I should like to emphasize the fact that while technically this may be described as a want of confidence motion, the real purpose of presenting it to the house is to seek to emphasize in every way possible the belief of hon. members supporting it that there is urgent need for action to deal with a situation which can no longer be glossed over.
I have no thought of following in the same vein the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat. We are not going to gain anything by seeking to surround this extremely important subject with political slogans or remarks of that kind. The attention of the government has been drawn to the fact that there is rising unemployment in Canada. There is some argument as to which set of figures should be taken. There are those who argue that the figures given by the dominion bureau of statistics of 362,000 are the correct ones. There are those who state that the figures should be those given of live applications for work. One brings us a figure of something approaching 400,000; the other brings us a figure approaching 600,000. I point out, Mr. Speaker, that in this particular case we find the heads of the large labour organizations, the chamber of commerce and other organizations in this country, appear to have reached a near approach to unanimity as to the seriousness of the situation and as to what they think the figures are. For instance, I find in Canadian Business, the official organ of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the statement that on the estimates which could then be made, following the trend which had been established, there are likely to be 600,000 applicants for employment in March. Those correspond with the figures which have been used elsewhere. They correspond with the figures that were given this week by the president of the Trades and Labour Congress, Mr. Jodoin. Here we find unanimity on that point. Whichever set of figures may be accepted, the fact remains that there is unemployment so extensive that it should no longer be disregarded by the government or by any other hon. member.
Last night and yesterday afternoon this house heard speeches by ministers of the

Unemployment
government. Yesterday afternoon the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), who followed the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough), after she had presented her extremely well documented and capable argument in support of the suggestion that immediate action should be taken to deal with this situation, said that we should not conclude the picture is all black. Certainly it is not all black. Nevertheless it is very black for a large number of Canadians, whichever set of figures you use. It is very black for those who are trying to find employment and have been trying for some considerable time.
Just as an example of what is coming to the attention of hon. members every day, I read in this morning's Montreal Gazette, as I am sure many hon. members did, a report of the Montreal presbytery of the United Church of Canada, made public yesterday. In that report we find these words:
Many families are in dire need now, and their number is increasing.
Farther on we find these words in the report:
The situation is actually so serious that every effort must be made to inform the Canadian people, who are living in relative prosperity, that a considerable group of their fellow citizens is out of work, and that many more will be facing a similar tragedy if immediate action is not taken to increase employment.
That is exactly what we are seeking to impress upon the government; that is exactly what we are seeking to place before the government, hon. members and the people of Canada by presenting this resolution at this time.
Last night the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) did not deal with the problem of unemployment. He gave an economic survey, painting a bright picture of the situation in Canada generally. Most of us will agree that the economic prospects in Canada are in most respects very encouraging. I doubt whether there is a single member of parliament who does not believe that this country offers to its people opportunities that are not exceeded in any other country in the world. Yes, there is prosperity. There is continuing prosperity. It is because of that prosperity that we are in a position to deal with this problem of unemployment. We are not in the middle of a world-wide situation such as that with which this country was confronted some years ago and which is within the memory of so many here. At that time there was a world-wide economic storm; conditions were very different, but today Canada with all its resources, with all its opportunities, finds

many of its people unemployed, not only at a time when many other people throughout the world need the things that can be made with our resources but at a time when other countries are enjoying a period of very high employment and very high prosperity.
Surely it is a startling fact that we in Canada should be worried about unemployment when other countries which only a few years ago were rebuilding their economies following the devastation of war are now finding it necessary actually to assist immigration into their countries to meet their employment demands. As an example it is not so long ago that many of us looking at the devastation in Germany immediately after the end of the second world war wondered how they would ever be able to rebuild their economy. In addition to the problem of restoring their producing capacity in Western Germany they were also confronted with the extremely difficult problem of handling some ten million refugees from East Germany who sought escape from the vile slavery of communism.
For a long time that seemed to present an insuperable problem for the people of West Germany. Today they have not only restored their producing capacity in West Germany to the point where the people who were living in West Germany at the end of the war are occupied; they have given work to thousands of refugees and they are now assisting immigration from Italy so that they may have enough workers to keep pace with the tremendous tempo of production in that area.
It is not so long ago since we heard people making rather gloomy predictions about what might happen in Great Britain. There were many discouraging reports about what was taking place there. Today the tempo of work and production in Great Britain is higher than it has ever been. There are less unemployed in Great Britain than there are in Canada, and that is not on a percentage basis but in actual numbers. According to the most recently available statistics there are more unemployed people in Canada although we have just over a quarter of their population than there are in Great Britain. Other countries are seeing great industrial prosperity and great demands for workers.
It is in the face of that situation that we call attention to the need for some action to deal with this problem. If there were 100,000 Canadians unemployed and who were actually seeking work and were able to work, we should be trying to find out how they can be employed. The lowest figure we have

is 362,000, and the generally accepted figure, except on the part of the government, is in the neighbourhood of 600,000. Let us not waste time about these statistics. The human problem is there of physically capable men and women wanting to work and not being able to find work in a country which has the power, which has the resources and which should have the initiative and the ability to create work by the combined efforts of our people.
Yesterday the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) made one or two comments with which I should like to deal. He did not seek to convey the impression that he was in any way dismissing this problem, but in his remarks he certainly conveyed the impression that he did not regard it as being unduly serious. Most certainly in the review that he gave he did nothing to remove the suggestion that has been left that this government simply regards unemployment as seasonal and regional.
He did say that neither Ontario nor any other province had indicated that unemployment had got beyond their ability to deal with it. Almost at the moment that he was speaking here, the premier of Ontario was meeting a delegation in Toronto. In this morning's edition of the Globe and Mail we find a report of a meeting between the Ontario government and representatives of the Ontario provincial federation of labour. I should like to quote from that report as follows:
The province has told Ottawa this, the premier said, and the Ontario government also has repeatedly expressed the view that any solution to the unemployment problem must be a co-operative one. All levels of government must share the responsibility, he declared.
The premier of Ontario left no doubt that he was anxious to deal with this subject. Further on the report states this:
Declaring that no level of government can take care of the unemployment problem alone. Premier Frost said the Ontario government is most anxious to sit in with representatives of all Canadian governments to discuss the problem.
Surely that is definite enough. I am under the impression that other governments have said the same thing. The premier of Ontario was dealing with those problems where there is overlapping responsibility. We know that there are cases where this government can deal with questions of unemployment when they are exclusively under federal control, but there are many cases where the federal, provincial and municipal governments all have their share of responsibility.
The Minister of Labour said that this problem is not one that has reached such proportions as to call for such vigorous action as
Unemployment
was demanded by the resolution or by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fair-clough) who spoke before him. Surely there is not an hon. member of this house who has not received letters and personal representations from his constituents and others indicating the real urgency with which this problem is regarded by so many thousands of Canadians at this time.
I doubt if there is an hon. member in this house who has not received pitiful letters from men and women who have worked for years and who now find it impossible to obtain work. They ask for any help that can be given to them in finding work with which they can support their families today. It is no answer to them to say that the country is prosperous. On the contrary, when they are told that the country is prosperous their natural reply is, "Well, if it is prosperous then let us see that prosperity extended so that everyone can feel the benefits of it".
I do seek to impress upon the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), upon the members of the government and upon the members of this house that the greater the appearance of prosperity with which our people generally may be surrounded, the greater the feeling of despair will be if there are ablebodied people who are earnestly trying to get work and cannot find it. What do they think when they see the very real prosperity which is evident? That can only lead to a sense of bitterness in their hearts that prosperity should be available to some and not to all.
The Minister of Labour was quite correct when he said there is no magic wand which can be waved to deal with this situation. I am not for one moment suggesting that any such magic can be applied. I am not going to follow any suggestion which may have been made here earlier that any hon. member of this house can offer a magic formula to solve this problem.
In this country we have three forms of government. We have the national government, which deals with national affairs and national problems. Under our federal constitution we have provincial governments, which deal with provincial affairs. Under the municipal acts passed by the various provinces we have municipal governments dealing with local affairs. Each one of these forms of government has its responsibilities at this time. As we have seen, it is not only the provincial governments which are confronted with difficulties. Only a few days ago I read a most significant report from the city of Toronto which was published in

Unemployment
the Globe and Mail of February 25. The heading is "Jobless Paid to Quit City and Go Home." The report reads:
Toronto welfare commissioner Rupert admitted to the civil welfare committee yesterday that his department had given funds to unemployed to leave the city.
Other Canadian cities were doing the same thing, he added.
In one instance, he said, the city of Regina, Sask., gave money to a Toronto unemployed family to return to Toronto.
I do not want to appear to be placing any unnecessary barbs in my remarks when I ask the Minister of Labour if that is what he is describing as "mobility". The minister referred yesterday to the fact that we have a rather satisfactory measure of mobility. Well, we do not want the kind of mobility which moves unemployed families from Toronto to Regina so that Toronto will get rid of the responsibility, and which moves unemployed families from Regina to Toronto so that Regina will get rid of the responsibility simply because neither municipality knows who naturally is supposed to deal with the situation. This is the situation with which we are confronted. Examples of this kind could be multiplied indefinitely. Surely, however, this does underline the difficulty which today faces municipal councils, provincial governments and the federal government here in Ottawa.
That leads us to the question as to whether something can be done to deal with this problem. Certainly something can be done. No matter what constitutional defects there may be in determining how taxes will be allocated and whether it will be one government or another which will handle a certain responsibility, we do know that either under the federal government or the provincial government anything that can be done by any government in any other land can also be done here in Canada as long as there is agreement.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And if there is the will to do it.

As the hon. member has added, there also has to be the will to do it.
There has already been discussion concerning various projects which would create employment and which at the same time would be useful to the Canadian economy. Undoubtedly some of these involve questions of jurisdiction as between one government and another. We have seen instances of that in proceeding with the tremendous developments on the St. Lawrence river. There were great problems to work out concerning that project not only between the governments of Canada and the United States but also between the provincial and state governments

as well. Those problems have been worked out although it took some considerable time. We know that if there is the will to do it and if there is a recognition of its necessity a solution can be found. This being the case, Mr. Speaker, this motion is placed before the house with the idea of emphasizing the very real urgency of the present situation. We ask the government of Canada to take steps which will meet this situation.
I notice that reference was made to the fact that this government would be prepared to consider ways in which the efforts of the different governments could be joined at a proposed conference between the federal and provincial governments to be held at some future date which has not as yet been stated. Mr. Speaker, that will be too late for many of the people in this country who are wondering today how they can live for the balance of the winter months. That will be too late for a number of the municipalities to know how to meet the problem which confronts them today. That will be too late for some of the provincial governments to know how to deal with the requests of the municipalities for a solution to the problem.
I believe we had an example last week of what is occurring in that respect. A delegation from the city of Toronto came to Ottawa to seek assistance with certain public projects there. They were told that this was not the immediate responsibility of the government at Ottawa and that they should first present their claims to the government at Toronto. The same sort of thing is happening all over Canada. Frustration confronts provincial governments, municipal councils and, above all, the individuals who are affected. It does not help very much the families of unemployed workers, who are waiting to know where their next meals are coming from, to be told that at some undisclosed date there is at last going to be a conference on taxation. That conference on taxation is long overdue. That conference on taxation will have many important problems to deal with. That conference on taxation will take some time to reach conclusions.
What is needed now is an immediate and vigorous approach to these problems on the part of those authorities who must deal with them. In all earnestness I urge the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) not to wait to write to the premiers with respect to the taxation conference before dealing with this immediate subject. This is something that should be dealt with right away. I am confident that if the Prime Minister sent a telegram to the premiers of every province in Canada and asked them to come to a conference immediately to deal with the problem

of unemployment and ways and means of meeting the situation, he would receive an affirmative response from every one of them without delay. That conference could take place within a week. It should take place within a week.
I think also that representatives of the municipalities should attend that conference. No one has placed more emphasis than I have on the fact that we must always respect our constitution and must remember that the municipalities are legal entities created under the municipal laws of the provinces themselves. Nevertheless some of these legal entities are very real entities. Their problems are very real and very immediate, as evidenced by the fact that municipalities are now providing transportation tickets to some families so that they will avoid the responsibility of caring for them while they are unemployed. I should think it would be highly desirable that representatives of the municipalities be invited as chosen by their representative association of mayors and municipalities, which embraces all urban municipalities across Canada.
Such a conference could then face the issue, find subjects that are common to them so far as this problem is concerned, and decide how this job can be done. Surely amongst men of good will, desirous of meeting the very real needs of the people of Canada at this time, a practical solution could be worked out in that way. I am not suggesting this as a substitute for the other conference which is long overdue and which will have the problem of dealing with the long-term aspect of many of the circumstances which themselves contribute to some of these difficulties. I do hope that conference will be proceeded with as quickly as possible.
I also wish to deal with this matter from the broader point of view. We are seeing increasing unemployment in Canada at a time when other industrial countries are actually finding it difficult to meet their employment needs. We are now in a highly competitive period which is going to continue. I am sure that everyone who has seen what has been taking place in Europe in the past few years has become impressed with the fact that we are going to meet the kind of competition that we have not faced for many years. It may be doubtful if we have ever faced as keen competition as we are going to see in the years ahead. I believe that Canadians can meet that competition. They can only meet it effectively, however, if they recognize the reality and if they join hands in every 50433-105
Unemployment
way they can to make our production efficient and to be able to meet this competition not only in the domestic field but in the export field as well.
The tempo of production in Britain, in Germany, yes, in many parts of France and in Italy, as well as in other European countries, indicates clearly that we will be well advised to make sure that we keep pace in efficiency and design with the best in every other land. One of the things that must impress every visitor to Europe at this time is the quality of the new designs in every type of industrial production. We would be well advised to encourage research in every field. In that respect I would urge the government of Canada to try to bring about co-ordination between the national research council, the various provincial research bodies supported and maintained by the provincial governments, and other research organizations so that we do not unnecessarily duplicate research tasks and so that we do explore every new field of opportunity to make use of the resources, the power and the skill that we possess in Canada. These are some of the long-term considerations that we must bear in mind. These are things which seek attention by joint action of the government of Canada and the provincial governments.
Let me once again come back to the question immediately before us. Able-bodied men and women are seeking work. Every one of us is receiving requests for advice and encouragement from many of these people. We are told that this country is prosperous. Let us hope it continues prosperous. The best way to assure that prosperity is to make sure that we avoid the unnecessary burden as well as the human anguish of unemployment in a country where the opportunities to create employment are so great.
I repeat my request that, in the face of the suggestions which have been made by provincial governments, by representatives of municipal councils, as well as by the many public bodies referred to by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) in her carefully prepared and comprehensive speech yesterday, the Prime Minister immediately- I mean immediately-extend an invitation to the governments of the provinces of Canada to meet here in Ottawa. I suggest as well that there be representatives of the municipalities in attendance, so that they may all tackle this problem and find some immediate solution, while at the same time seeking a long-term solution of which this country is undoubtedly capable.
It may not be possible, Mr. Speaker, to wave any magic wand. It most certainly is

Unemployment
not. It may not be possible to create employment overnight. Nevertheless, hope is always a wonderfully comforting thing to those who are confronted with despair. At the moment those who are seeking employment cannot find it or any evidence of anything that is to be done which will give them the employment they want. What we are urging in presenting this resolution is that the government take action which will produce results and which will also raise the spirit of our people, whatever the number who may be seeking employment now, by giving them reason to believe that here in Canada those charged with public responsibility recognize the seriousness of the situation and will do everything they can to meet it in the way this country undoubtedly can.

I did not want to interrupt the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), Mr. Speaker, but he did ask me a direct question to which I thought he wanted a reply. He asked me whether the workers who, according to the press, were being sent from one city to another because the city could not give them assistance, were the people to whom I referred yesterday in commending the mobility of labour. In answer, may I say I did not refer to them. I was referring to those Canadian workers, mainly without deep roots in any community, who were willing to go into our hinterland and work for the development of our country. I deplore, as much as he does, the plight of those to whom he referred.

I have oeen here throughout the debate, and I listened with particular attention to the spokesman for the official opposition, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough). I must confess that she lost me in statistics and after a while she got lost too.
Oh, I don't think so.

Her reference to the labour publication, "Why Wait for Spring?", as drivel was not lost on the house or on the country. The pamphlet has for its purpose the furthering of government efforts to attack seasonal unemployment. The principle underlying the pamphlet can be stated as follows: renovate and repair during the winter, which is the slack season for the building trade. This principle has been endorsed by the three labour congresses, the Canadian Construction Association, the Canadian Manufacturers Association and the Canadian Retail Federation. They have all joined to further the attack on seasonal unemployment, and they have partaken in eight broadcasts on 77 stations, time free.


These broadcasts were undertaken by the leaders of those organizations, along with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) and others, who prepared and gave the broadcasts. There have been requests for more than 5,000 scripts and requests are still coming in. Anne Francis, the well-known commentator, did a broadcast entitled "Why Wait for Spring?", the name of the booklet. Immediately there were requests for 665 copies of the script. This was considered to be unusual and was no doubt due to the charm which was added to the content. In addition there were 25 women's organizations that participated by publicizing the principle of the pamphlet to their members. To this list can be added the Hamilton-Brantford branch of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Hamilton chamber of commerce and the Hamilton construction association. I believe the professional and business women's club in Hamilton will be doing something about it in a week or so.
What was the result of all this? Here is a report that appeared in the press, dated Port Arthur, February 15:
The national employment service here has figured out a way to help the unemployment problem.
Service officials asked residents last week to have small jobs done during the seasonal lull of unemployment rather than wait for spring or summer. The result of the do-it-now drive: more than 500 tradesmen and labourers who normally would have been out of work have something to do.
The spokesman for the Tory party calls that drivel.
A dribble is right.

They repeat that "drivel" is right, although 500 people are employed in one city. Let me get back to the problem of the unemployed. I do not think the discrepancy in the unemployment figures is important. There is not much comfort in either set of statistics. In any event, the unemployed are not statistics. I feel, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) pointed out yesterday, the important thing is that we are again confronted with a figure for unemployment which has now reached the postwar peak. Just when we thought we had achieved our goal of full employment, it appears to shimmer away. I do not think we need to quarrel about terminology. It does not matter whether you call it regional, seasonal or cyclical, it is still unemployment. These people suffer in unwanted idleness and in need.
There are some things that need to be said on the plus side, and they must not be lost sight of by this house. There are 140,000 more persons gainfully employed in 1954 than

there were in 1953. One of the chief difficulties is that our economy is not keeping pace with our growth in population. If another job was not lost, not another person was laid off, unemployment would still rise in this country in the absence of the growth of our economy. It is obvious that either our economy must expand or the unemployment rolls will. On the basis of everything that had gone before, we expected the growth in our economy would parallel the growth in our population; but that has not been so. Despite the number of those who have no employment in Canada today, there are employed in this country at the present time more people than at any other time in our history.
That, too, must be on the plus side.
It is beyond argument that Canada today enjoys the confidence and goodwill of foreign investors to a degree never before experienced. This is attributable to the climate created by government policy. We have witnessed and we are still witnessing a tremendous influx of foreign capital into this country, which is proof of the high regard in which we in Canada are being held, as a long-term risk. There is no reason why we should be selling this country short.
No criticism of this government is valid if it seeks to blame its trade policies for the rise in unemployment. We have endeavoured consistently to free trade from the entanglements of barriers; and at GATT we have raised our voices in disagreement with those who would perpetuate a system which can only hamper reciprocal trade. Canada has enhanced its reputation in the eyes of the world by its consistent advocacy of the demolition of barriers and other impedimenta to reciprocal trade. We have pioneered in that field. We must continue to cry out against any trend that would erect barriers around nations to the detriment of their own economy, and the economy of those who wish to buy and sell.
We think there is benefit for all in world trade. We have given GATT more than lip service. This house, too, must remember that since 1945 the government has embarked upon a program of social expenditures that might be likened to economic shock absorbers. They have removed many of the bumps from the economic highway along which we have to travel. We have tripled our expenditures in the field of what is termed social welfare, from $425 million in 1945 to $1,200 million in 1953. This huge outpouring of money from the national treasury, which would have been undreamed of a few decades ago, has acted as a true stabilizer in the post-war years. It has flattened out the unemployment dips. It has

Unemployment
stimulated buying power, and it has served to restore public confidence.
The outlook is not a grim one. Public and private investment in 1955 is expected to show an increase over 1954. The figures tabled by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is seldom wrong, indicate an increase of 3-84 per cent over the 1954 expenditures estimated at $7,841 million. His down to earth speech in the house yesterday did much to restore an atmosphere of confidence in the country. People in this country will remember well these words, when he said, "We can expect 1955 to be a very good year."
In addition to that, the allocations the house will be asked to approve for public works will be greater than ever-an increase of more than 10 per cent. The construction industry, always a sensitive barometer of unemployment, had a record year in 1954 and confidently expects that 1955 will be still better. The government is entitled to a lot of credit for its progressive and far-reaching policies in this respect.
When the building industry was being throttled for lack of funds the government pioneered in a new field, and enlisted the aid of the chartered banks as lending agencies for the building of homes. Now the home improvement section makes it possible for home owners to obtain loans at reasonable-rates.
All this has been done by a government which has been alert to the needs of the day. But we find ourselves at this time with very-large numbers of unemployed. And so novr a tresh counter-attack on unemployment is necessary, and much more requires to be done. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce indicated yesterday, some supplementary measures will have to be taken. To accuse this government of being indifferent or blind to the needs of the people is political expediency. This government has a long and distinguished record written in the acts of parliament and in the hearts and minds of the people. It has shown great and vital concern for human needs, and does not intend to live on laurel leaves. There are many of us whose minds go back to the bitter thirties and we know what the people suffered then!
We are determined not to permit it to happen again.
When are you going to start?
We have started. As a matter of fact employment is on the upturn this month as compared with last month.

You said that in 1929.

Unemployment
What figures do you get that from?
From the people; they know when they are employed.
From Liberal meetings?

I cannot hear everybody when I am interrupted, but I am willing to listen if you will speak one at a time.
Sometimes forgetful but never unmindful; sometimes diverted, but never indifferent to the plight of human beings who are being punished for no other reason than that they want to work, and have no work for their hands.
But this must be said, if one is to take an honest appraisal of the situation. Too long have governments at all levels regarded unemployment as some sort of mirage that would vanish with the spring and with the summer sun before anything positive had to be done. Today unemployment of course is not a mirage; it is bigger and more ominous than ever. It will not disappear because we will it to vanish. To us it is a problem, but for the man who loses his job, it is a calamity.
While for most people there is employment and a very high level of income, side by side with that prosperity there is want. Consumer goods are being sold in record quantities; houses are being erected by thousands, and there is no lack of buyers. Everything points to good times, and yet in the midst of this abundance we have want; and this want is not static. It is a spreading disease for which a remedy must be found; and if anyone can find it, this government can.
Foremost and most immediate is the man who is willing and able to work and for whom no work is available, whose benefits are exhausted. For him the situation has reached a critical stage. His purchasing power is virtually nil. For this man yesterday's wants are today's needs. I cannot overemphasize the gravity of the situation as it affects the employables who are jobless. It took us many years to recover from the fibre-rotting experience of the great depression. I know, as do many other hon. members, what prolonged periods of unemployment can do to the human soul. We have indeed progressed little if we permit to happen to the man of 1955 what happened to his father in 1930. This man has been buffeted and pushed around in a jurisdictional dispute, not as a matter of deliberate policy, of course, but that has been the end result.
There is one body in this country that sees the dangerous trend and its implications, namely the Canadian Welfare Council, which recently issued an invitation to all senior levels of government to meet in April to
[Mr. Hodgson.l
informally discuss assistance to the unemployed. The council is acting as an honest broker in this respect, and its effort to obtain action from the senior levels of government is commendable. But one would have thought that federal-provincial relations were on a sufficiently sound basis for action to be initiated within the governments and not be left to an outside body, even one as competent as the Canadian Welfare Council.
As the matter now stands, the provinces are free to approach the federal government on the problem of assistance for the unemployed, but the basis of the approach has never been clarified. Will the government assist when the burden has become too heavy for the provinces to carry, or when it is merely heavy? At what stage do we come in? Yesterday the Minister of Labour did clarify the government's position. He said, "When it reaches the proportions beyond the capacity of the provinces to deal with." I was very downhearted when I heard him say that, but he corrected it in a later part of his speech. He clarified the statement by saying that it is a matter for discussion at the dominion-provincial conference, if the provinces want to discuss it. Well, it is no secret that the provinces now will want to discuss it, and so progress has been made in that it certainly will be on the agenda and will be discussed.
Is that enough? That is what we must ask ourselves at the present time. Recently the province of British Columbia did make an offer to the dominion government to divide the cost on the basis of 40-40-20, the 20 to be paid by the municipalities. That was neither accepted nor rejected. I think British Columbia was asked to assess its problem in detail and advise the government, which it has not done to this date.
It is my own feeling, from whatever experience I have had on this subject, that we should have accepted that offer or perhaps made a counter-proposal by saying that we would be prepared to pay on the basis of one-third each. The acceptance of the offer or a counter-proposal which might have been accepted would have ended the vagueness which surrounds the question, and it would have served to establish a precedent and a pattern. I think the time has come now to spell out the basis of federal participation, at least an interim basis for participation. We have to do something; otherwise we simply pile up misery for the unemployed and grief for ourselves.
We read alarming stories which tend to confirm doubts about the prosperity of our times. We hear-and this story is quite common and true-of fathers deserting their families in

order that the families might be eligible for public assistance. Then there is the heartbreaking evidence of parents putting their children out for adoption because they have no food for them. Press reports indicate that fathers have committed deliberate acts of violence to have themselves arrested and sent to jail so the family may be provided for.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) made reference to another matter that I am going to deal with. Public bodies are beginning to buy one-way tickets for the unemployed. Toronto admits that it is shipping unemployed to their former homes where there are no jobs available for them, and Regina and other cities are sending unemployed back to Toronto where there are no jobs available for them. Other cities are doing the same thing. It costs much less to buy a one-way ticket than to give someone assistance, so the merry-go-round has begun.
These people are citizens of a province; they are Canadians who have been pushed and shoved around as though they were something less than human. This is a base, cruel and unjust interference with personal freedom. Because they are destitute there is no reason why they should be deprived of their fundamental rights as Canadian citizens. There is one thing that should come out of this debate, and that is word to these various provincial and municipal authorities that this has to stop.
The voluntary agencies have just about reached the end of their tether. They have been doing a magnificent job, but this is a task for senior levels of government; the voluntary agencies have not the resources. There is need now; there is an immediate need, and it cannot wait until spring or summer. They cannot wait until such time as the dominion-provincial conference is called. They need help now.
It is my own view that we, who claim the prior right to tax, have the prior obligation to provide employment opportunities, or in the alternative to contribute in case of need. Let me pinpoint what is happening. In Toronto employment insurance benefits paid in November, 1954, to those entitled to receive them amounted to $1,200,000; in December to $1,600,000; in January $2,000,000; and in February to $2,600,000, or a total of $7,400,000. That is a lot of money; yet it is only a fraction of what those people would have received if they had been gainfully employed. All this money created no jobs, turned no wheels; it was money for subsistence on a primary level. It bought food and paid for some other necessities, but it created nothing in itself.
In the 1930's we spent millions on unemployment relief, and when the emergency
Unemployment
ended there was nothing to show for all our expenditures. I remember one year when Ontario spent $48,000,000, and in the end we had people who were bitter and broken. I suggest that today we have the opportunity to strike a positive blow at unemployment by embarking upon a most imaginative and far-reaching public housing program the like of which Canada has never seen before. We need low-cost houses and rental houses. We have the labour force ready and willing to work. We have an abundance of materials and all the necessary know-how, and there is no lack of money.
In Toronto and other large cities in Canada there is a need for slum clearance and redevelopment. Why not give additional assistance by way of financial aid to such projects and when normalcy returns, as we hope it will soon, we will be able to point to concrete accomplishments brought about by the expenditure of these vast sums of money. If the provinces are reluctant, or cannot or do not want to undertake any of these projects, the finances of this government are such that we can do it on our own account.
Housing brings with it a demand for materials, equipment and household furnishings. The construction industry has not yet solved the problem of winter building, claiming climate is the reason. I feel that is just an excuse. It is about time the construction industry, which has been a beneficiary of this government, should be told, "Climate be hanged; get out and build". They can do it. I admit that there are places in Canada where winter building is impossible due to extreme weather, but that has not been the case this year in Toronto and the larger cities in the southern part of Ontario. Forty per cent of the Toronto unemployed are construction workers.
The truth of the matter is that the climate is not so bad in Ontario and Canada but that the climate is better in Florida and the Bahamas where most of these builders are at the present time. That is why building in Ontario has slackened up particularly at this time. The builders are so busy trying out their new Cadillac cars to find out if they will do everything the salesman said they would. The salesmen said that they would do everything except fly and talk back. The result is that they have not had time to carry on continuous building activities.
The major causes of our unemployment are lack of consumer purchasing power, the drop in farm income and the loss of foreign markets, principally the latter. The drop in farm income has backed up to manufacturing

Unemployment
Ontario. We too feel its effect. I think it is a thunderous indication of our interdependence and the important part that primary producers play in our economy.
Due to our phenomenal growth and the stability of our economy the Canadian dollar now enjoys a premium on the world market. I use the word "enjoys" advisedly. This premium has been fairly constant up until recently at 3 per cent. While the premium has been good for our ego, it has been far from good for our export trade. For some time we have realized that it is a luxury which we cannot afford, because it adds to the cost of doing business. Doing business in the world market today is difficult if you have to get a premium on your money. Recently the government through the Bank of Canada reduced the interest rate on loans to chartered banks, which in due course will mean cheaper money to the public. In addition we have been buying United States dollars on the open market and redeeming some securities in the United States before their due date. All this has had a tendency to lower the premium, and I notice that today press reports indicate that the premium is less than 1 per cent.
But our dollar is still subject to strong external pressures. Not only must we bring it down, but our dollar must be kept at parity with the United States dollar. Otherwise the same article will cost more than its United States counterpart. So far so good, but there is one sure way to do away with the differential between our dollar and the United States dollar, and maintain the Canadian dollar at par. This can be accomplished by doing some deficit financing in our budget this year. I would have hesitated to use that word in this house a couple of years ago, but not now.
I raise the matter of deficit financing, and by that I mean substantial deficit financing which by some of course may be considered inflationary. We may be accused of passing on a greater debt to our children to pay some time in the future.
Are you flying a kite now?

I am always accused of flying kites. I am just saying what is in my mind. The prospect of deficit financing does not frighten me and I do not think it should frighten others, because we have people in our government who used to be called bureaucrats and who know something about handling inflation. They are still available if we should need them.
We must not lose sight of the fact that in countries where there are less bountiful IMr. Croll.]
natural resources, increased debt may be a burden, but to us it can be only an incident on the road to expansion and achievement. There is no reason for us to be panicky, but this is not a time for half measures either. The fiscal policy to be announced in the budget must embody bold, courageous and decisive measures. I know there is always a tendency and temptation at budget time to give everybody a little, but with the large body of unemployed in this country we must channel our tax benefits where they will give stimulus to employment.
I suggest that there are two approaches to this problem. The first is to give the public a sizeable reduction in personal taxes and thus increase consumer demand and consumer purchasing power. I am aware that consumer spending has been high, but I am one of those persons who believe that it is a good thing to put money into the people's pockets even if it does not buy quite as much as they think it ought to buy. It has the added advantage of letting people spend their own money in their own way, and that is good for their morale.
Hear, hear.

The wrong people in the house are agreeing with me. The second approach is to give manufacturing business in the export field which is capable of job expansion and growth some special concession. I have in mind accelerated depreciation.
Business needs two things. I do not hesitate to be earthy when I say that it needs a shot in the arm and also a kick in the pants. It needs a shot in the arm by way of stimulus and incentive, and it needs a kick in the pants in order that it may be reminded that it should stop being smug and self-satisfied and should get busy. They are no longer order takers for goods in short supply; they must get out and hustle as others are doing in this very competitive world and who, in the export field, are running rings around our own people. I am not advocating that we grant business generally a larger share of tax relief, because it would not be beneficial to employment since commercial and financial corporations deal in services and do not add greatly to job opportunities.
The manufacturers who export say that the loss of markets is due to the fact that they cannot be competitive. They say the Canadian standard of living, excelled by no other country save possibly the United States, has placed them at a disadvantage in the foreign export market. To lower that standard is unthinkable, so we have no other alternative except to widen the basis of our economy by creating more jobs. Granting an incentive of

accelerated depreciation to manufacturers who produce for the export market, in the same way we now grant accelerated depreciation to those plants engaged in defence work, would make it possible for them to cut their production costs as a result of this tax saving.
At present the Minister of Defence Production provides a certificate indicating whether the whole or a portion of a plant is used for defence production. An accelerated depreciation, which is a considerable benefit, is granted to that portion of the plant which is engaged in defence production. The problem of unemployment is surely as important and far-reaching as defence. In solving that problem we build up our home defences. Thus if we do away with the differential between our dollar and the United States dollar, and give the export business an accelerated depreciation, there will be a reduction in the over-all cost. This will make it possible for our exporters to compete in world markets. It will also assist them to stay in the export business, so that at least we will not lose more markets in the future. It is quite possible that in time the tax department will recover the accelerated depreciation from these plants, because they can obtain the write-off only once and their profits are subject to taxation at a later date. A further advantage is that, unlike road building and other public works, the employment in these manufacturing plants is continuous. At this point I would like to say that such financial aid to job-creating business would be extended for the single purpose of creating employment, and must not be regarded as a source of profit for shareholders.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is of the utmost importance that we as a government give the lie to the accusation that free enterprise works only in times of war; that it knows how to produce for destruction but not for consumption, and that it cannot cope with the problems of equitable distribution. The past has given some support to that criticism. It is a challenge to us to show that we are capable of coming to grips with the nightmare of a swelling army of jobless men.
We have made hard decisions on the international front in recent months. These were decisions that were arrived at with difficulty and not without misgivings. In making these decisions we acted on the basis that realism demands realism. On our domestic scene, too, we must face realistically the hard realism of spreading unemployment. We cannot accept unemployment as a way of life inherent in the free enterprise system. I have oversimplified the problem in saying we need to create 100,000 new jobs a year for many years
Unemployment
to come in order to provide for the new people who join the labour market. I believe the present government can perform that task better than any group or any combination of groups in the opposition. The present government has the experience, the know-how, the courage and the will to take such steps as are required in order to bring this scourge of unemployment to an end.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when one follows a speech such as that which has just been made by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), one wonders which part to follow. During the early part of his remarks he seemed to be doing his best to persuade us that there is no real problem so far as unemployment is concerned. He admitted that some of the speakers we heard yesterday had left him in a state of confusion concerning figures, but he contributed to that confusion in attempting to prove that the problem is not as real as the unemployed know it to be.
The hon. member followed the practice which is frequently pursued on the other side of the house of trying to lull the unemployed to sleep with a dream of the glories of the Liberal party and all the wonderful things its apologists claim it has accomplished for the people of Canada.
But even so ardent an apologist for the Liberal government of the day as we have in the hon. member for Spadina found that in the course of his address he had to put down the sheaf of notes on the basis of which he indulged in glowing adjectives concerning his party and pick up another sheaf of notes which seemed to deal with the undeniable fact that there is the hard realism of spreading unemployment about which something must be done.
I congratulate my hon. friend on recognizing that the problem is still there, even after he tried to wave his magic wand and get rid of it. I noticed that even in the mor,e realistic part of his speech, in which he admitted that there is an unemployment problem, he felt the blame must not be put upon the government which he supports but must be put upon private enterprise. He suggested the blame should be put upon the builders and contractors who drive about in their big Cadillacs and who are wintering in Florida or in the Bahamas. Surely he has been in this house long enough and has been an observer of and participant in the Canadian political scene long enough to know that in Canada the final responsibility for the economic climate rests upon the governments of this country, and particularly upon the federal government. No one on the Liberal

Unemployment
side has any right to stand up and claim credit for the Liberal party for any of the things which seem all right if he is not prepared at the same time to take the responsibility for that party and that government when things go wrong.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. friend who has just taken his seat was completely correct in that part of his speech where he admitted that we have an unemployment problem, where he asserted that something should be done about it and that this should be done right away.
It is certainly not my intention to add to the figures which have been placed on the record yesterday and today in considerable quantity and in a manner which, I think it is fair to say, has created some confusion. In the main I think that confusion has been created by persons like the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the hon. member for Spadina, who have tried to analyse the figures in such a way as to suggest that there really is no problem of unemployment. There is one fact which these figures do underscore, and it is that we have in Canada today the greatest amount of unemployment that we have had since the end of world war II; and no amount of analysing these figures by the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the hon. member for Spadina or any of the other 169 Liberals with whom we are blessed in this house-
