speechtext:
You can look it up in the dictionary and see that it has various meanings-will bring any comfort to the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are at the present time unemployed and suffering the consequences of that unemployment.
The amendment now before us has two points of emphasis, and I think all of us who recognize that there is an unemployment problem realize that those two points of emphasis are equally important. On the one hand, it is extremely important that something be done immediately to deal with the situation as it affects hundreds of thousands of Canadians right now. It is no help to the unemployed, particularly those for whom there is no financial assistance or utterly inadequate financial assistance, to tell them that correspondence is being exchanged between the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the provincial premiers

with a view to holding a federal-provincial conference some time in 1955. So far as these people are concerned action is needed, as others have said in this debate, right away.
I must say to the Minister of Labour that I was disappointed last week when he seemed to feel that the fact that he had not heard directly from Mr. Jodoin was sufficient excuse for not having done something about the proposal of the president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada for a threeway conference of government, management and labour to deal with this important matter. Likewise I was disappointed last week when it seemed so difficult for those on this side of the house to persuade the Prime Minister that something should be done right away about the invitation issued by the Canadian Welfare Council for a conference of the senior levels of government with that council to discuss the problem of assistance to unemployed persons. Surely the government does not need to wait for proper invitations written on the right kind of letterheads, sent by registered mail, or what have you. Surely the problem is there in sufficiently staggering proportions that the government, having failed to take the initiative along these lines itself, should at least lose no time in responding to the kind of suggestions these bodies have made.
I support as strongly as I can those who have urged in this debate that conferences of the kind that have been suggested be held immediately to try to meet this problem in terms of aid or work right now for the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are suffering unemployment. At the same time I want to urge that emphasis be placed on the long-range aspect of the amendment that is before the house. Even though it is a long-range aspect, and even though I shall say something that is long-range in character, it is my conviction that the long-range effort should get under way immediately.
The plain fact of the matter is that there is a great abundance of things to be done in this country. We have the raw materials, we have the resources, we have the labour. Indeed, the hon. member for Spadina was spelling these facts out in the better part of his speech, and I suggest it is utterly unthinkable that in a country with the resources and labour power we have on the one hand and the needs we have on the other there should be any unemployment whatsoever.
So, Mr. Speaker, I rise to suggest to the government as strongly as I can that consideration be given right away to a 12-year program. Someone may ask why I suggest

a 12-year program. Well, add 12 years to 1955 and that brings us to 1967. I am suggesting that we seize this crisis not only as something that should be dealt with because of the urgency of the immediate problem, but as an opportunity to launch a crusade to change the face of this Canada of ours so that by the time we celebrate our 100th anniversary it will be the kind of country we know it can be and believe it ought to be.
I call upon the government to give leadership in a crusade between now and July 1, 1967, to make of this country a much better place than it is at the present time, not only for the more than half a million who are unemployed but for Canadians from coast to coast in many ways that I could detail. I urge this on the government despite the fact that some members of the government may say they know they are not going to be over there for another 12 years. That is one good thing which I know they will admit. Some members of the cabinet may feel that father time is against them, and that they may not be around for 12 years in active political life; but surely the mark of statesmen is to think of the future, and even though the government or individual members of the government may not feel that they are going to be active leaders in this country for any great length of time, surely it is their responsibility to think in these terms.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the proposal I make this afternoon, and I am going to spell out ten or a dozen fields in which things can be done that are sorely needed in this country which would change the face of Canada and put us in a position so that, on July 1, 1967, we can really celebrate our 100th anniversary as a nation. I think hon. members will also realize that the things I am going to suggest would provide so many jobs in the meantime that instead of having unemployment rolls we would be looking for people to do the work.
The hon. member for Spadina said, in one of the better sentences of his speech when he was talking in realities rather than in adjectives, that our economy must expand or the unemployment rolls will. That is my text, if you will, right from the speech of the hon. member. My proposal is that our economy must expand, and that what is needed is leadership on behalf of the people of the country by the government of the day. I am satisfied that if any crusade such as I am suggesting is launched by the government now occupying the treasury benches there is no question but that it will catch the imagination of the Canadian people, and that any 50433-106
Unemployment
government that is over there after the next election or the election after that will carry it on.
The first effort which I suggest in this 12-year program is in fact in a field that was referred to by the hon. member for Spadina, namely the field of housing. Some day soon we must get over the notion that because we have national housing legislation, because houses are being built for those who can afford them, we have met the housing problem in Canada. As long as there are slums in Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg or Vancouver we are not ready to celebrate the 100th anniversary of Canada on July 1, 1967. Why not do something about it? Why not resolve that by that time there will be no slums in any of these cities or in any other cities of this country? It can be done if I may quote what has been said earlier, if there is the will to do it. I call upon the government to set a slum clearance program at the top of the list, not just on a hit and miss basis, not just here and there when the municipalities can afford to come into it, but as a positive crusade to make this Canada the kind of country it ought to be.
During the 12-year period to which I have referred we should have as our goal to see to it that every Canadian is decently housed. Let us accept it as axiomatic that just as we already agree that every child born in Canada is entitled to the best education we can provide, so every child born in this country is entitled to a good home and good housing. For a goal I suggest that, in addition to the 100,000 houses per year being built at the present time, we might aim at another 100,000. I would suggest that we might break that total goal of 200,000 housing units per year into two parts, 100,000 for home ownership and 100,000 subsidized low-rental homes. This program would call for some new thinking about the legislation that is now on the statute books. The 75-25 formula will not provide for the building of 100,000 low-rental units per year.
No one denies that we need homes in these numbers. It is a fact that we need a building program of this magnitude. The governments of this country, federal and provincial, have it in their power, as the Leader of the Opposition said earlier today, to do anything that can be done provided there is the will to do it. I suggest that the proper housing of our Canadian people should be at the top of the list in this 12-year crusade which I call upon this government to launch.
I suggest that particular attention should be paid to the housing of our senior citizens. I have had occasion to refer once in a while to some of the projects that have been established in some parts of this country. I think

Unemployment
of the projects established in my own city under the leadership of the Reverend Fred Douglas of old St. Andrew's United Church. I think of a project of which I know at the coast, of one in Windsor and in other places. I suggest that real consideration should be given to the provision of housing for our senior citizens. Let us not have it in July, 1967, that any senior citizen could be living in the kind of housing we read about in some of these very well written feature articles that have appeared in western newspapers lately describing the plight of our old age pensioners. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Spadina put so much emphasis on this matter of housing which in itself, as he pointed out, provides tremendous opportunity for creating employment, not just so as to put people to work but so as to meet the needs of our people and make Canada a better country in which to live.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I move on to the second group of things to which I feel real attention should be given. We should include in our crusade the manufacture and production of the things that are needed in the homes we have today as well as in the homes I hope will be built in the next few years. My leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), pointed out last night that according to the 1951 census we need right now 2 million furnaces; 2 million refrigerators; 1-5 million toilets and bathrooms; 1 million washing machines, not to mention all kinds of appliances and equipment of that sort or the things that go into the adequate furnishing of homes for decent living in this country. There is a tremendous field for production and for employment in that area.
The hon. member for Spadina can complain about private enterprise not doing it. The fact of the matter is that they have not done these things. These things are needed. We want a better Canada, and we want to get rid of unemployment. I suggest that in so far as this matter is concerned, the federal government should take the lead. It could announce such a crusade at a meeting of the various governments, the welfare council, labour and management, such as has been proposed during the last week or two by some of these interested bodies.
I move on to the third item in this 12-year program which I call upon the government to launch, and it is in the field of highways. I am not going to waste any time on the argument that roads are a provincial responsibility. We know there are these dividing lines. We know also that we can get together and work out an arrangement based on the underlying principle that in Canada parliament, either dominion or provincial, is
SMr. Knowles.]
supreme. Anything that needs to be done can be done, under the direction of one or the other of these senior governments, so long as there is the will to do it. I call for a real speed-up in the completion of the first trans-Canada highway. I threw in that word "first" advisedly, because I suggest there is room for a second trans-Canada highway, certainly in western Canada as well as in parts of eastern Canada.
In addition to the work that could be done and the advantages that could come from the completion of the first trans-Canada highway and the building of a second one, there is a tremendous need for connecting roads. I think of the kind of roads that could connect our trans-Canada highway and our main centres with the United States. I think also of the market roads and other kinds of roads we need in our provinces as a whole. My seatmate, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), has on occasions told this house something about the highway program in the United States. He has spoken of the federal administration and the part it plays in that country's highway program, even though highways are under the states more or less as they are under the provinces in Canada.
Here, too, is a great field for employment and for improvement of this country. When we spend energy and raw materials on things of that nature we are not making ourselves poor; we are making ourselves richer. The production of goods that we use or that enhance our life or that make our country more beautiful is all to the good. We are adding to the wealth of the country, and there is no reason why things like these should not be done.
I move on, Mr. Speaker, to the fourth category of things that are sorely needed in this country, and I admit that they are to a considerable extent at the municipal level. Let us not hold up progress in this country; let us not delay building the kind of Canada I think we all want, by the time we celebrate our 100th birthday, by quarrels over jurisdiction. Surely we can get together with the municipalities, either directly or through the various provincial governments, to discuss with them ways in which the federal government could help the municipalities meet some of their needs today. A few days ago I referred to the need in the city from which I come for a number of bridges, and I mentioned particularly the Disraeli bridge over the Red river in downtown Winnipeg. We also need another bridge over the Assiniboia river. These are needed because of traffic congestion in our city.

These things are beyond the financial capacity of a city, but something could be done at this level with federal aid. I mentioned the Disraeli bridge for Winnipeg, but I am sure that in the minds of others there might be the Marpole bridge in Vancouver, the bridges and tunnels requested for Montreal, as well as bridges and other works that are needed in other cities in Canada.
Further, it is not out of place for us to think of the parking problem that has become acute in every city in this country. I recall the day, Mr. Speaker, when even the mention of the trans-Canada highway in this house was regarded as out of order. I recall Mr. Speaker Glen stopping members from discussing that in this house because it was a provincial responsibility. We have moved on, and we realize that even though matters are of provincial or municipal responsibility the federal government can come into the picture, at least in terms of financial assistance. There is something that can be done if we can just get together on it, to find ways and means of relieving the heavy parking problem we have in many cities. There are these and other things at the municipal level that I urge should be included in the program of a 12-year crusade.
I suggest a fifth proposal that would be all to the good for this country. One of the things in which we are rich in Canada is scenery. We have lakes, rivers and woods, and out west we have the clear blue sky. Hon. members who live in this part of the country probably miss it, because they do not have here the blue sky we have on the prairies.
But while we have tremendous resources in terms of beauty for the people to enjoy during holidays, and though we have increasing numbers of people who have a bit of time off from their work during holiday periods, the fact of the matter is that resorts and camps are still reserved largely for the well to do.
I call upon the government to give leadership in a program involving the building of camps and tourist facilities, to make it possible for all Canadians when on holidays to get away from the cities or the farms to some of the many beauty spots found in Canada from coast to coast. Let us accept something like this as one of the things that should be part of life in this twentieth century, and let us try to have something like this done in time for that significant event, the celebration of our 100th anniversary as a nation on July 1, 1967.
My sixth proposal is that, without any further delay, without any further jockeying, and without any more trips back and forth to 50433-106i
Unemployment
Regina by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the federal government should join with the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba in setting up a Saskatchewan river authority similar to the Tennessee valley authority, so that it might enter upon a program of conservation of soil, water and forests in the whole Saskatchewan river area.
I call upon the government to give that authority power to build the South Saskatchewan river dam, with all the advantages it holds in terms of power and irrigation. This year the problem in the west has been too much water rather than too little, but we all know that unless something is done there is danger of drought in the future. Let us avoid that by a vast project such as would be envisaged in the South Saskatchewan river dam. There, too, we have an opportunity to provide employment and an opportunity to change the face of agriculture for the better for a great section of the western prairies.
My seventh proposal is that there should be a similar authority for the Assiniboine and Red river areas. From time to time we have had problems there, notably the serious flooding in 1950. But on other occasions we have had too little water in the Assiniboine and Red rivers valleys. Here, too, there is room for conservation and room for improving generally the economy and the wealth-producing capacities of that area. There could be co-operation between such an authority and the international joint commission so that we might put the economy of that area on the best possible basis.
I include with this proposal one similar to it. I suggest that for the British Columbia area, for the slopes of the Rockies, there should be authorities with real power to enter upon necessary programs of conservation and reforestation. Again a tremendous field for employment would be opened, and a tremendous step taken to improve the wealth-producing capacities of this country and make our country one that will prosper for a long time as a result of having looked to the future and practised proper conservation procedures. It has been highly significant that there has been great interest in a resolution dealing with this matter which has been presented to the house from time to time by my colleague the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). I suggest the interest shown in that matter indicates that the house generally would be behind the government in all these proposals for the conservation, care, and proper development of our great natural resources.
Likewise, as an eighth proposal, I think we should have an authority to deal with the

Unemployment
conservation problems of the Ontario area, problems which have already been discussed in the house. An authority similar to the ones I have just mentioned would be required to deal with the South Nation river, the Grand river, the Thames, the Etobicoke and others. Here again there is a tremendous field for improvement.
The hon. member for Spadina said, "Let us capture the imagination of our people in the field of housing." He knows how thoroughly I agree with him in that. I say, let us capture the imagination of our people with a 12-year program and really set out, not just to solve the immediate problem, important as it is, but to place our economy on a vibrant and growing basis so we will not be back next year or the year after dealing with unemployment. How much better it would be if we were coming to the house year after year and saying to the government, "You must go out and get more workers." There is no reason why that should not be possible; and it would be a lot happier problem with which to deal than the problem of unemployment confronting us today.
Let me suggest still another project, a ninth proposal; and in doing so I cannot help taking a glance at my friends to my left because, when I mention it, I know I will have their support. I think it is time the railway connecting the Peace river district to the Pacific coast was constructed. It is nine years now since the house passed a resolution along those lines, but still nothing has been done. And I think, too, of the dream the Minister of Agriculture had one time about a railway running across northern Canada from the Peace river area to Hudson bay. I do not think it was a nightmare, either. That is another project that could be on the books in the 12-year program I am suggesting.
My tenth suggestion is that particular attention should be given to the economy of the maritime provinces. We all know that for many years the chief exports of the mari-times have been youth and brains. We know that across the years there has been a tendency for maritimers to go over to Boston or up to other parts of Canada. For many years that has been accepted as standard practice for maritimers, but it seems to me it is not a condition that should be accepted at all. When one thinks of the timber resources, of the coal deposits, of the iron ore in the Ungava district, of the possibilities in farming and fishing, he must conclude there is no reason whatever why the economy of the maritime provinces should not be put on a basis where life would flourish down there and be just as vibrant and progressive as it

was in the days of the wooden ships which, of course, were the glorious days of the maritime provinces.
As some hon. members know, I speak with interest about that part of the country because my parents happened to be among those who in their youth left the maritimes to go elsewhere. They were only doing what many maritimers have done across the years. I suggest there is tremendous room for economic programs in that part of Canada that would put people to work and at the same time change the face of the country so that, as I suggested earlier, when July 1, 1967, rolls around, we will have something to celebrate.
If we do not launch upon a program like this and, as the hon. member for Spadina has said

and he was perfectly right-if we do not expand our economy, the rolls of the unemployed will expand. And what a celebration it will be in 1967 if we find ourselves with a million unemployed. All the speeches and the flag waving the leaders of that day might indulge in would not fill the bill.
You will note that though I have listed 10 different categories of projects that could well be launched, I have not exhausted the field, and I have not referred to some matters that might be regarded as highly provincial in character. Surely we can find some way, though, to provide money for the building of schools that are sorely needed in some areas in particular in this country. I mention last, perhaps for the top of the list, so far as I am concerned, the question of health. The room there is for the building of hospitals, clinics, medical colleges, dental schools and nursing schools is beyond the imagination. We need them sorely; we cannot afford not to have them. I think the people of Canada want a health program that really takes care of our health needs. I suggest that this be included as the crowning plank in a 12-year program such as I have proposed.
I am just about through, Mr. Speaker. I am not going to take any further time to deal with the question that somebody is bound to ask, as to how the cost of this is to be met. I have answered that question as I have gone along. When you apply labour to raw material and create new wealth, you do not run the country into any real debt. You increase the country's wealth, and that is what these projects would do. It would make us a stronger and wealthier Canada 12 years from now than we are today.
If a war broke out tomorrow, which is unthinkable, even if it were a 12-year war we would meet the cost. We would meet it by the production of extra wealth, by producing things we are not now producing. That is what I am asking for in a war on unemployment, in a crusade for a better Canada. We

do not need to take away from any wealth we now have in Canada. We can create new wealth along the lines that I have suggested.
Mr. Speaker, I call upon this government not just to ask the unemployed to settle for tributes to the fine way in which they have taken the unemployment they have had to endure. I call upon this government not to ask the unemployed to find comfort in the statistics and assurances given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. We can do better than that. Let us give them the tools. Let us give them the goal of a better Canada. Let us get on with the job.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the last speaker, and I can agree with him wholeheartedly when he claims that there is no justification for an unemployment problem in this country; because if we ever put into circulation the various products that are so urgently needed in Canada today and at the same time maintained the purchasing power of the people to buy the goods they wanted there would be no question of unemployment. Probably in a short time there would actually be a shortage of labour.
At the food and agriculture conference at Rome in the fall of 1953 it was pointed out that the paradoxical situation of the 1930's was again becoming prevalent in the world, evidenced on the one hand by the degree of poverty and starvation that existed in many parts of the world, and on the other hand by the large surpluses occurring. For instance, I noticed in the Journal yesterday a reference to the fact that the surplus of food in the United States has now reached the staggering proportions of $7 billion. I noticed that a letter from the welfare council of January 28, addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), pointed out that there was also a paradoxical situation in Canada where we had a large number of people suffering from want as a result of unemployment.
They put the figure of the number of people affected by unemployment as approaching 30 per cent of the total labour force. I am not going to argue about statistics. It is not very important whether it is 30 per cent, 20 per cent or whatever the figure may be. The point is there are a very large number of people in Canada today suffering, and suffering severely, as a result of unemployment; and that is happening at the very time when the national income of Canada is at a near all-time high.
There is no question but that the difficult agricultural situation in western Canada has had an adverse effect upon employment, especially upon the implement industry. I am
Unemployment
hoping that at this session the government will take action to amend the Agricultural Prices Support Act to establish a sound formula for setting support prices. Recommendations have been put forward by the various farm organizations. I am satisfied that if the government will act upon those recommendations it will help to maintain agriculture on a sounder basis, and thereby help to provide a better market for eastern produce shipped to western Canada.
I think all hon. members will agree that the present situation is undesirable. I hope all hon. members will agree that it is a situation that need not exist. Furthermore, I hope all hon. members would agree that no time should be lost in taking action to relieve that situation in the quickest way possible. I would say that it is a somewhat sad reflection upon the intelligence of the government that after science has been able to bring about a superabundance of goods in this country, the government has failed up to date to provide the means by which that superabundance can be made available to the people. Therefore as unsold goods accumulate production is curtailed and unemployment expands. Twice already this session we have had ministers rise in their places and say that while it would perhaps be very desirable to take action along the lines suggested by the opposition to deal withi such problems as increased payments under-the Unemployment Insurance Act or increased' payments of family allowances, the government should not take that action because it would cost too much money; they could not afford it. I never expected to hear that state

ment again in this house, because for four or five years we never heard that expression once.
There was a period in this house when at the time we were dealing with serious problems we considered just one thing. We considered whether we had the men and the materials available in this country to deal with the matter; and if we had the men and materials available and it was considered that they could give better service in dealing with that problem than with any other, whatever money was needed was always made available. At no time during the war did any minister rise in his place and say we could not do this or we could not do that because we had not the money. As I say, there was just one thing under consideration, namely whether or not we had the men and the materials to execute it.

What is physically possible is financially possible.	j..~

Exactly, provided that it is desirable.
And intelligent, too.

I say, no minister ever rose in his place and said that. On the other hand, it is interesting to note that the Leader of the Opposition did take a different stand. At that time the leader of the official opposition objected to the high level of taxation and suggested that it might be wise to decide how much we could afford to spend and then limit the war effort to that number of dollars. I am glad to say it was only the official opposition and not the government who took that stand; because had this government and all the allied nations adopted that policy, then I do not think there is any doubt that we would have lost the war.
We fought a war to attain an objective. The objective we had in mind was to establish peace in the world and make a high standard of living available to the people. In order to reach that objective, we did have fo adopt a realistic financial policy. Well surely, having reached that objective, we are not going to fail or refuse to adopt the necessary financial measures to make that objective work.
That is what we should be doing at the present time.
What is the situation in Canada today? We have the situation that goods are being produced faster than they can be sold; not because they are not wanted by the people but rather because many people who want those goods are unable to buy them. In other words there is a lack of effective demand in Canada today. So industry tries to persuade the people to buy more goods. We have full page advertisements in the press; we have sales put on throughout the stores; we have announcements that $1 will permit you to take home this refrigerator or $5 will permit you to take home that electric stove, the remaining payments to be made on easy terms.
Largely as a result of this type of advertising, and largely as a result of the expansion of credit, buying on credit in Canada has reached the very high level of $1-8 billion. What would have been the situation if that credit had not been made available? That merely illustrates that for the people to buy the goods they have bought they had to go into debt to the tune of $1-8 billion, and that does not take into consideration the longterm loans made under the National Housing Act and other such schemes. Yet in spite of that heavy credit buying we are still unable to sell our total production. Consequently in many lines production is being reduced today and unemployment is increasing.
[Mr. Gillis.f
In the past after a prolonged period of peace the unemployment problem has invariably been solved by war. It might be argued, perhaps, that large-scale unemployment is a softening up process to get people willing to support war. I noticed last year an editorial in the Calgary Herald headed "An Astonishing Reason for War". It quoted President Eisenhower as saying:
The President pledged that the United States would never go to war to solve the unemployment problem. Prosperity under the Democrats, he said, was based on war. The Republican government, he said, would do everything possible to find jobs for those out of work.
We find this horrifying, and we think perhaps millions of decent Americans will find it horrifying too.
The editor says, "We find this horrifying." He was horrified at the suggestion that unemployment might influence nations in going to war. President Eisenhower is not the first president of the United States to make that statement. Hon. members will recall that after world war I Woodrow Wilson stated that the deep-rooted cause of war was hot industrial rivalry for foreign markets, which are the other side of unemployment. There you have two presidents frankly admitting that unemployment or the fight for foreign markets has been a cause in bringing about wars.
I recall how during the Korean war the U.S. News and World Report, when giving its forecasts, repeatedly stated that the amount of money that would be expended in the United States to carry on the war in Korea would be just sufficient to maintain a high level of employment. In other words the Korean war was being used as a stop-gap method to maintain a high level of employment. That is no doubt the reason the war in Korea had to be a limited war for an unlimited period of time, because it was being used merely for the purpose of taking up the slack. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) has put these quotations on Hansard on a number of occasions, so it is not necessary for me to deal with them now.
I think it is quite obvious that unemployment in Canada today is largely due to a lack of effective demand, a lack of domestic markets. In the final analysis the domestic market is the only market we have, because our imports are brought in in exchange for our exports and the local market has to absorb the imports brought into this country in exchange for our exports. So you have to have an effective demand against your total production available for distribution within the country, and exports do not in any way change that situation; they merely make it possible to exchange one product of which we

have a surplus for another product that we need. They do not reduce the amount of goods that have to be sold within the country. If you want to maintain full employment you must do something to provide markets.
Lack of purchasing power.

The hon. member for Cape Breton South says it is a lack of purchasing power. That is something we have been voicing in this house for a number of years. Many people ask why there is a lack of effective demand, why industry is not self-liquidating. Surely when industry operates at a high level and pays out salaries, wages and dividends, that purchasing power should be sufficient to buy the total output of industry. We have always argued that the reason there is a lack of effective demand is that owing to certain practices inherent within the present system, industry is not able to maintain an effective demand against its own production except in times of abnormal capital goods construction, such as we have in wartime, in the development of a new country or during a period after war when we are rehabilitating the damage done by war.
Let me give a brief explanation. Under private enterprise most of the new production is financed by savings. It is quite obvious that when money is paid out by industry a certain proportion of that money is going to be saved. To that extent there will be a lack of purchasing power available to buy the total output of that industry. People will generally admit that is true; but they will say, "Just a minute, that money will be invested in new production which will be paid out in salaries and wages, and therefore will become available to buy the goods which were left unsold." That is true, but on the other hand, having produced new goods there will have to be money available to buy the goods in that new cycle of production, and if you use that money to buy the goods left unsold in the last cycle it will not be available to buy those in the current one and goods will be left unsold to that extent.
I could give a simple explanation, but I think the matter is quite obvious. It is not necessary for me to say anything more on that point, except that it has been recognized by many leading economists that investment savings and investment are bound to cause a deficiency of purchasing power. That is recognized by Maynard Keynes and Professor Soddy, and was recognized in the national survey of potential productive capacity in the United States which was carried on under the Hoover administration. More recently it was recognized by the president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce in his 1952 annual
Unemployment
statement. I notice that members of parliament seem to pay far more attention to what a bank manager says than what is said by another member, so I shall just quote what the president said in that report:
If it is agreed that gross national production should as a minimum be sustained at present levels, then deterrents both to personal and corporate saving (investment) require immediate and careful examination. Income cannot be redistributed for consumption and at the same time invested to expand productivity without some serious strains developing.
And further on:
Increasing consumption, both domestic and foreign, is necessary if the heavier volume of goods and services arising out of our enlarged capacity to produce is to be absorbed.
It is quite evident that people cannot spend their money on consumer goods and at the same time invest it. It is not merely a question of sustaining the present level of production; we must extend our production in order that additional income will be available to the expanding population. But what is the use of encouraging people to save and invest if as a result of their saving there is a lack of effective demand for the expanding supply of consumer goods?
It is interesting to note that in a more recent edition of the report by the same bank they stress the fact that from now on we should put the greatest emphasis upon the need for expanding consumption in this country. I would also point out that it is important that we maintain a proper balance between investments in productive and nonproductive industries. If we reached a situation where we had expanded our plant and equipment to such a point that it was capable of providing all the goods the people required, the right thing to do would be to divert our investments to non-productive enterprises in the form of national projects, bridges and railways or anything that does not expand the supply of consumer goods.
It may be argued that if the analysis I have made is correct then the system would have crashed long ago; if industry is not self-liquidating how is it that industry has continued to function for all these years? I would say it is not necessary for the industrial system to crash so long as there is a steady expansion of debt. As long as we are willing to expand debt in order to finance that deficit, then of course the system can continue to operate indefinitely until we reach the point where we have to borrow the money to pay the interest.
It is interesting to note the rapid increase in debt. It is also interesting to note that when we attempt to curtail credit or reduce debt we find ourselves entering into recession. It is interesting to note that the debt

Unemployment
in Canada, for instance, increased from $3-7 billion in 1939 to $17-25 billion in 1952. Foreign investment in Canada increased from $6 billion in 1926 to $10 billion in 1952. Of course that investment creates a drain upon our production. Federal debt in the United States increased by $11-4 billion in the last five years.
If we are prepared to allow the debts of the country to climb indefinitely we can, of course, make the system work; but there always comes a time when the people become fearful of an increase in debt. At those times we have people saying "It's dangerous; the government should do something about it. We have to have a balanced budget and increased taxation." The people do not seem to realize that if you increase taxation you reduce purchasing power and the amount of purchasing power available will be still further decreased.
It is only necessary to refer to the history of the past to prove the truth of what I have said. Let us consider what happened in 1914. There was a recession at that time, and then we had war and an expansion of debt which was followed by a few years of prosperity. In 1930 there was a curtailment of credit which was followed by a depression. In 1939 we had war, credit expansion, and then a few years of prosperity. In 1949 we were reaching a slow-down. In 1950 we had war in Korea, prosperity, and an expansion of debt.
Once again we have a slow-down. One might well ask, "Where do we go from here?". Of course if we have another war the situation will clear itself, because there will be no difficulty in obtaining whatever money is necessary to maintain a high level of employment. However, I think most of us realize that another war is out of the question. Another war would solve the problem by eliminating mankind; therefore there would be no question of unemployment. It is quite obvious that today we cannot depend upon another war to maintain the economy in a state of equilibrium.
Therefore the sooner we take action to deal with this situation the better it will be for all concerned. We in this party insist that to the extent the money paid out by industry fails to maintain an effective demand for its own production or imports, additional money should be paid by the federal government to the consumers to maintain the balance. So long as the amount of new money is sufficient only to bring about the balance there is no real danger of inflation. In other words, if our objective is to develop the resources of the country, including manpower, to make available to the people as high a standard of 
living as this country is capable of supplying, we must see to it that sufficient money is paid to the consumer in order to maintain an effective demand.
It is interesting to note that the rather orthodox newspaper, the London Economist, placed that statement clearly before its readers. I quote from page 182 of the August 11, 1945 issue of the Economist:
The condition of full employment as is now universally recognized is that the economy should generate a sufficiently large flow of effective demand to purchase the whole of the gross national product. In simpler language, somebody has to buy the volume of goods that full employment will produce, or they will not be produced.
The quotation ends at this point, but I of course would add the statement that unemployment will then increase. The April 14, 1954, issue of the Saturday Evening Post carried an interesting article by Mr. Ben Pearse entitled "Ike's Depression Doctor", a statement made by Mr. Frank Burns, chairman of the council of economic advisers to President Eisenhower. He says;
As our economy expands to supply the growing needs and wants of our growing population, we want to keep our capacity to produce things, and people's financial ability to buy them in as close balance as we can.
He disagrees with those who claim that we have too much plant and equipment now.
To support this generally prosperous situation there has already been a 10 per cent tax cut, the first of the year, and others will come as government spending is reduced. The administration program also urges that social security benefits be broadened and increased, and that unemployment insurance in many states far below its originally intended purchasing power be modernized.
I think today there is a greater understanding of the fact that if we wish to maintain our economy in a high state of flux it is absolutely essential to maintain the purchasing power of the people at a level which will make it possible for them to buy the total production of the country.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) placed before the house this afternoon a number of recommendations. I would like to refer to those recommendations and comment briefly upon them. The first recommendation dealt with the elimination of the sales tax and wider use of the price discount. I think we all realize that in a situation such as we have today we want action and we want it fast. It does no good to talk about a dominion-provincial conference to be held in June. It is not enough to say that we will wait until spring, so employment can increase. In order to expand the purchasing power of the people we want some action that can be taken almost overnight. We suggest that the first step would be the elimination of the sales tax, which would increase not only the purchasing power of the individual but also the

purchasing power of the dollar in the hands of the individual. There is no doubt that would help to increase demand.
The second recommendation concerned the assumption by the federal government of financial assistance to those unemployed not covered by unemployment insurance or extended benefits, and the expansion of payments for social services such as family allowance, old age pensions and war veterans allowances. This is similar to the recommendations that were made by the Canadian Welfare Council in 1953. The council set up a committee to make recommendations dealing with unemployment, which were considered by the organization across Canada. At a meeting in Ottawa the recommendations were finally approved by the board of governors on December 13, 1952 and were published in 1953.
The first recommendation pointed out the need to increase employment. The second and third recommendations dealt with changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act. I shall not deal with those recommendations now, because that act will be revised during the session. The fourth recommendation concerned rehabilitation programs for ablebodied and disabled persons, and pointed out the need for the development of rehabilitation programs. I shall now read the fifth, which we agree with:
(a)	The federal government should assume most of the financial responsibility for the residual assistance required by all employable unemployed persons not provided for adequately by unemployment insurance or extended benefits.
(b)	The federal government should fulfil this responsibility by the purchase of service from other authorities-that is, by payments to each province for the assistance and services given by it, or by its municipalities, to these people.
(c)	The federal payments should consist of a basic payment and a variable payment: (i) the basic payment should be a percentage of the cost of administration of the entire general assistance program at the provincial and local levels; (ii) the variable payment would be the federal government's share in providing for the employable unemployed, the amount being determined at any time by a formula through which the amount of general assistance given to this group is ascertained.
Then there is this comment:
The federal government should, without delay, enter into negotiations with the provinces to carry out this recommendation, in order te provide for the residue of the employable unemployed which exists in "normal" times and to establish the machinery by means of which adequate provision would be made in "abnormal" times.
As I say, we agree with that proposal.
Then I come to our third proposal, a vigorous employment policy with government assistance to private industry to absorb seasonal unemployment.
That might take effect in many different ways. I think we would all agree that it is
Unemployment
important to do everything we can to increase employment at a time of seasonal unemployment. In my opinion a great deal could be done to encourage construction in winter. The main trouble is that it is more expensive to carry on construction in winter than in spring, and therefore many firms and people defer their building until the springtime. We are of the opinion that the government would be justified in actually subsidizing a part of that increased cost in order to encourage business to build in winter instead of waiting until summer.
Many of us have seen what is happening in Ottawa today down on O'Connor street. You see a steel frame erected. Then you see them spread tarpaulins around the frame, put heat and light inside and continue with their building. Having reached the first floor, they then move the tarpaulins up to the second floor, put in heat and light and continue their construction. No doubt that type of construction is far more expensive than construction in the summer or spring, and therefore I think the government would be fully justified in helping to subsidize construction of that kind rather than allow the people who are doing that type of work to remain idle. It would be far cheaper for the country, because by subsidizing we would have an increase in wealth, and it would be actually cheaper than paying out unemployment insurance.
This is our fourth point: A program of construction of national projects with emphasis on those works that can be carried on during the winter months.
Of course there are many national projects that can be put under way not merely for the purpose of providing employment but in order to provide the services that are so urgently needed in Canada today. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to a variety of projects that are needed in Canada. I could mention two or three in which I am quite interested. For instance, in Saskatchewan there is the South Saskatchewan river dam project. We have not heard very much about it lately, but I have the idea that as the next election approaches we will hear more and more about it both from the government side of the house and from our side.
In my own constituency we are very interested in what is known as the Red Deer river diversion project. That project would make it possible to irrigate half a million acres, and the estimated cost of the project is only $15 million. The main purpose of that irrigation project would be to provide feed lots. It is largely a livestock country, and the trouble is that while there is enough feed for stock in

Unemployment
the summer there is often no feed in the winter, because they cannot grow enough feed on account of it being too dry. If we had irrigation we could have feed lots. Feed could be raised and there would be feed to carry over the stock in the winter. It is a really worth-while project which might well be called self-liquidating.
Then there is the elimination of level crossings. I think every hon. member could give the government a list of projects that he considers should be executed at the earliest possible date. I was a member of the reconstruction committee which sat after the last war. We built up a shelf of projects. I do not know what has happened to them. I think most of them have fallen off the shelf or have been forgotten.
Then I come to the next point in our program:	5. A support price program for
agriculture. I have already mentioned that. Recommendations are being made by agricultural organizations to the government for [DOT]changes in the formula under which agricultural prices are set. I think the government would be well advised to give careful consideration to these recommendations.
6. A more realistic trading policy which would involve the acceptance of some foreign currency in exchange for Canadian goods, and which would involve amongst other things the revaluation of the Canadian dollar. I have for a number of years criticized in the house the maintaining of the Canadian dollar at the present high level, but naturally not very much notice was taken of what I said. However, I am glad to see that today, now that the president of the Royal Bank is advocating the same thing, more attention is being paid to the matter. He warns of the danger of the present high level of the Canadian dollar, and points out that it puts us under adverse competitive conditions with countries whose currencies are depreciated below the level of ours.
I shall not say any more about the recommendations, except to mention that on a number of occasions we have advocated the acceptance of another nation's currency in payment for a certain proportion of our exports. We have to compete with the United States. Today the United States, as the result of a bill passed last year, can sell up to $1 billion of agricultural produce in exchange for the currencies of other nations. We have to compete with that nation, yet we are in a very adverse position to do so when they are able to accept foreign currencies and we insist upon payment in dollars.

I suppose the question that comes immediately to the minds of hon. members with respect to a program such as I have suggested is how it could be financed if it were to be put into operation without expanding the debt or without extending taxation. We have not suggested at any time that taxation should be abolished so far as the income tax is concerned. We have advocated that the sales tax should be abolished, but the income tax should be maintained because it is needed to provide an equitable distribution of income and services within the country. We say, therefore, that to the extent that limited borrowings of the savings of the people and an equitable system of taxation fail to provide the government with necessary funds, the government should finance through the Bank of Canada. It is interesting to remember that at the last session of parliament we amended the Bank Act to provide for a variable cash reserve. Now the government can finance through the Bank of Canada, and if it is feared that the chartered banks will use this new money for further credit expansion the cash reserve requirements of the chartered banks can be expanded to whatever point is necessary in order to prevent that happening.
Let us ask ourselves this simple question. If war broke out tomorrow would there be any hesitation on the part of the government in providing whatever money was needed to bring about immediately the full development of our resources in order to fight an all-out war? I think most members would agree that there would not be any hesitation at all. We have only to go back to what happened in 1939. From 1935 to 1939 we had been urging upon the government in the house the necessity for putting more money in circulation to provide for a greater degree of employment and social services. The cry had always been that the government could not do so because it did not have the money. Yet within a few months of the declaration of war the government got the chartered banks to create for their use $200 million in new money. It is interesting to note the reason the then minister of finance gave at that time for this expansion. I quote from page 140 of Hansard of September 12, 1939:
All this is not to say that a small and carefully regulated amount of credit expansion may not be desirable in the early stages of the war in order to assist the increase of production and employment. It must be small and carefully controlled because its effects which may not appear immediately are cumulative and otherwise might get out of hand. If at the beginning of the war there are unemployed resources, some credit expansion may give an impetus to their prompt utilization.

That was to justify the creation of $200 million of new money to provide for full employment. What happened in the next four years? Over $4 billion of new money was created in order to make it possible for the government to pay the increased costs arising out of the all-out war effort. The only voice raised in opposition to an all-out war at that time was that of the leader of the official opposition.
Now, it is often argued that an expansion of money is bound to be inflationary. It is true that in wartime you have an inflationary complex; that is to say, as soon as war is declared people are afraid there will be a shortage of goods and therefore they start to lay in a supply. They start to buy heavily. Although not even one new dollar has been issued, from the day war is declared people start laying in supplies because they are afraid that later on they will not be able to buy all the goods they want. This has nothing to do with financial policy. On the other hand, expansion in wartime is inflationary for the simple reason that money is used for the production of war materials. When salaries and wages are paid out for the production of war materials, those salaries and wages cannot be used to buy what has been produced for war, so those salaries and wages become a demand against the restricted supply of consumer goods.
In peacetime that will not be the case. In peacetime, especially when you have unemployment, you could use the expansion of money to bring about the expansion of consumer goods. Those salaries and wages paid out by industry for the production of consumer goods would become demands against those goods. The expansion of money, therefore, for the purpose of maintaining full employment in peacetime is not anything like as inflationary as it would be in wartime. So today, Mr. Speaker, we advocate that just enough new money should be issued and paid out in order to equate demand and supply. There would be no danger of inflation, and in that way the program we have suggested could be financed with little difficulty.

As it is now nearly ten minutes to six, Mr. Speaker, and I have something to say that will take more than 15 minutes, may I move the adjournment of the debate?
On motion of Mr. Hees the debate was adjourned.

I am rather inclined to agree with the hon. member. I believe we might dispose of the matter more readily if we continued with it than if it were allowed to stand over. So far as the official opposition is concerned, we would go along with the suggestion.
I feel exactly the same way. If the government could see fit to carry on this debate tomorrow, we might finish it. I would prefer it that way.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I am always glad to accommodate the opposition if they have a common mind. We did fix Thursday for the external affairs debate at their request, and now they want to change. I find it difficult to keep up with these changes of mind. For that matter, it should not be assumed that there is not some reason for having the external affairs items sent to the standing committee at a fairly early date. This debate is not going to be wound up tomorrow; I am sure no one would say that. I am quite sure hon. members opposite are not likely to agree to wind it up on Friday. I have been told this debate will run into several days, and I expect it will. Let no one believe that we could have a vote tomorrow night if we went on with this tomorrow.
Now, in view of that, if my hon. friends feel that they do want to go on tomorrow and will do what they can to shorten the speeches and get on with a decision about these things, we would be glad to accommodate them. But I do not think the government should be asked to set aside the time of the house for an unbroken period when,

Business of the House
in fact, there are still a good many things that should be started so they could be cleared off at a later date. I am not trying to minimize the importance of the debate on unemployment at all when I say that.

I may say that the external affairs committee is very busy with Bill No. 3, so it will not make any difference to that committee. I am very happy to know that the minister agrees with suggestions that have been made from this side.
